headline: Several marketed blue-light blockers may miss LED wavelengths relevant to evening-light reduction.
implication: Supports requiring spectral/fidelity guardrails before treating a product as suitable for the bedtime protocol.
caveat: Bench optical study; no sleep, melatonin, or adherence outcomes.

headline: Yellow lenses did not improve simulated night pedestrian detection
implication: The bedtime protocol should not imply tinted lenses improve nighttime visibility; users should prioritize safe movement in dim rooms.
caveat: Yellow night-driving glasses are adjacent, not the same as red glasses used while stationary before bed.

headline: HEV-filtering spectacle lenses may transmit substantial blue/cyan light.
implication: Supports separating mild HEV-filtering products from strong pre-bed circadian-light filters.
caveat: Bench lens-transmission study without biological outcomes.

headline: Blue-light-blocking coatings reduced but did not eliminate short-wavelength transmission.
implication: Supports caution that coating-only products may be inadequate for bedtime circadian-light reduction.
caveat: Short optical measurement report, not a sleep or melatonin study.

headline: Blue-blocking lenses can reduce blue colour contrast sensitivity
implication: Protocol safety language should acknowledge possible color/contrast visibility tradeoffs.
caveat: This is an acute visual-performance result, not a sleep outcome.

headline: Blue-light filtering lenses can alter speed perception
implication: Protocol guidance should discourage visually demanding tasks while wearing strong red/blue-blocking lenses.
caveat: The tested lens types and task are not the same as bedtime sleep use.

headline: Student feasibility study showed high adherence and no reported adverse events, with preliminary efficacy signals.
implication: Supports feasibility and safety framing for a home protocol, but not definitive efficacy.
caveat: Small feasibility design was not powered for efficacy.

headline: Orange blue-blocker lenses prevented bright-light melatonin suppression in an acute nighttime study.
implication: Mechanistically supports requiring high-filtering amber/red lenses rather than weak clear computer lenses.
caveat: Acute laboratory melatonin-suppression study, not a home sleep-outcome trial.

headline: Blue-light hazard marketing should not be conflated with evening circadian-light reduction.
implication: Supports conservative claims and safety language for strong filters in dim or task-critical settings.
caveat: Narrative perspective; not a bedtime glasses efficacy trial.

headline: Blue-blocking filters did not clearly reduce digital eye-strain symptoms
implication: Avoid using digital-eye-strain relief as a promised benefit of bedtime red glasses.
caveat: The intervention was a filter during a task, not red glasses before bed.

headline: CBT-I adjunct glasses study is clinical supervised context, not standalone protocol evidence.
implication: Supports clinical-adjunct boundary language and symptom-outcome context; do not use as direct home-protocol efficacy.
caveat: All participants received CBT-I; objective sleep duration did not improve in the active group.

headline: Short-wavelength-blocking bedtime eyewear source remains adjacent/context-only.
implication: Use cautiously for adjacent bedtime-eyewear context unless full extraction supports direct status.
caveat: Small study and adjacent lens variant; exact effect sizes were not extracted from accessible metadata.

headline: Blue-blocking filters did not alleviate signs or symptoms of digital eye strain
implication: Keep eye-strain relief out of core protocol claims.
caveat: Screen filters are not red bedtime glasses and the task exposure was short.

headline: Blue-blocking screen filter did not improve visual discomfort or accommodation
implication: Avoid translating screen-filter results into promised bedtime eyewear comfort benefits.
caveat: Filter/screen task, not glasses before bed.

headline: Workplace field studies are occupational adjacent context, not direct bedtime sleep-biomarker evidence.
implication: Adds real-world functional context and chronotype moderation only.
caveat: Occupational outcomes and incomplete extracted sleep effect sizes; not a dedicated sleep-biomarker trial.

headline: Longer-term blue-blocking lenses did not show contrast-sensitivity loss in extracted results
implication: This can temper safety concerns about some lenses, while still requiring product-specific visibility checks.
caveat: Not a sleep trial and not red-lens bedtime use.

headline: Ophthalmic-lens review supports conservative clinical-claim boundaries
implication: Use to avoid broad blue-filtering lens claims in the protocol page.
caveat: Detailed extracted effect estimates were not available in this batch.

headline: Broad systematic review found promising sleep-onset evidence but heterogeneous mood evidence.
implication: Useful for landscape framing and subgroup boundaries, not for a single pooled protocol estimate.
caveat: Heterogeneous designs and populations; includes uncontrolled studies and conference abstracts.

headline: Bright evening light suppresses melatonin and increases alertness
implication: Supports the rationale for reducing bright/short-wavelength evening light before bed.
caveat: Not eyewear-specific; it tests light exposure geometry in a laboratory automotive setting.

headline: Blue-filtering IOL review does not justify consumer macular-protection claims
implication: The protocol page should not borrow retinal-protection claims from IOL literature.
caveat: Surgical IOL evidence is a major population and modality mismatch.

headline: Radiology resident pilot was directionally positive but underpowered
implication: Treat as adjacent exploratory evidence, not a confirmed protocol benefit.
caveat: Small occupational sample and sham comparison; not sleep-focused.

headline: Pre-bedtime light is associated with longer sleep-onset latency
implication: Supports tracking and reducing pre-bedtime light as a plausible experiment signal.
caveat: Observational association; do not claim causal eyewear benefit.

headline: AMD/pseudophakia filter study highlights low-light visual-performance cautions
implication: The protocol should flag eye disease and low-light mobility as caution zones rather than claiming safety for everyone.
caveat: Special clinical population and acute tasks; not bedtime sleep evidence.

headline: Abstract-only meta-analysis reported mixed objective and subjective effects.
implication: Use only as historical context and do not rely on it over full-text syntheses.
caveat: Abstract-only; participant count missing; one reported CI/p-value combination appears inconsistent.

headline: Monocular/night-work partial-filter study is an implementation guardrail only.
implication: Use for coverage/binocular-dose guardrails, not bedtime sleep efficacy.
caveat: Not a bedtime sleep trial; night-work and monocular filtering are adjacent variants.

headline: One adjacent computer-use study suggested eye-fatigue benefit
implication: Preserve this as a mixed adjacent finding, not as a direct red-glasses-before-bed claim.
caveat: Participant count/effect estimates were not extracted here and the context is computer use, not sleep.

headline: Blue light filter task-performance findings were mixed with more visual fatigue
implication: Protocol language should separate performance, comfort, and sleep endpoints.
caveat: No participant count was extracted and this was not a bedtime intervention.

headline: Short-wave filters may improve glare/photostress in pseudophakic patients
implication: This is clinical context, not general protocol efficacy; it supports population-specific caution.
caveat: Pseudophakic clinical sample and visual endpoints only.

headline: Photostress effects depend on stimulus and do not justify broad claims
implication: Use for visual-performance boundary language, not for sleep or safety superiority claims.
caveat: Small acute study with normal-vision younger adults.

headline: Conference abstract is same-mechanism context, not direct trial evidence.
implication: Supports mechanistic plausibility only; full methods and participant data were not extracted.
caveat: Participant count and full methods/statistics were not extracted.

headline: Tinted lenses can trade contrast gains for color-discrimination losses
implication: Protocol safety language should not assume red lenses are visually neutral.
caveat: Small, older acute study; not a sleep intervention.

headline: Longpass-filter visual-performance testing is a safety context source
implication: Useful for considering task visibility when selecting red/amber lenses.
caveat: No extracted sleep outcome and detailed effect estimates were not captured here.

headline: Pilot insomnia study linked nocturnal amber lenses to working-memory and sleep improvements.
implication: Adds cognitive-context support but should be counted carefully because it overlaps the insomnia lens trial evidence.
caveat: Small pilot with possible practice effects and no multiple-comparison correction.

headline: Shift-worker guideline is general boundary context, not protocol support.
implication: Can support shift-work separation and general light-management context only.
caveat: Consensus guideline; not a red-glasses trial and not general-population evidence.

headline: Retinal-protection mechanisms are not consumer protocol efficacy evidence
implication: Use only to explain why eye-health claims require direct evidence, not as a claim source.
caveat: Narrative, older, and not bedtime-eyewear evidence.

headline: Direct adult bedtime-eyewear registry, but no extracted effect result
implication: Useful for locating and checking a direct adult glasses trial design before making protocol claims.
caveat: Do not treat the registry listing as the trial result or merge it with publications without explicit identity matching.

headline: Digital-eye-strain review is context, not bedtime-eyewear evidence
implication: Separate screen-related eye comfort from the evening-light sleep experiment.
caveat: Narrative review and not intervention-specific for red glasses.

headline: IOL retinal-protection evidence has important limitations
implication: Use as an appraisal caution for macular-health claims, not as protocol evidence.
caveat: Commentary/evidence-analysis and a modality mismatch.

headline: PROSPERO actigraphy meta-analysis registration is endpoint context
implication: Useful for deciding which objective sleep signals to track in evidence appraisal.
caveat: Registration-only source; do not treat as the completed meta-analysis or as a pooled result.

headline: Wearable endpoints need bias-aware interpretation
implication: Useful for deciding which self-experiment sleep-tracker signals are plausible and which are too device-dependent.
caveat: Adolescent PSG validation source; not an adult light-reduction trial.

headline: Mechanism review supports plausibility, not eyewear efficacy
implication: Can explain why evening blue-light reduction is biologically plausible while keeping claims bounded to direct trials.
caveat: Narrative review; no bedtime red-glasses intervention result.

headline: PROSPERO registration tracks nighttime blue-light-reduction review scope
implication: Useful for evidence-landscape traceability before citing the completed review separately.
caveat: Registration-only source; no effect estimate or pooled result is extracted.

headline: Blue-depleted room light has positive supervised signals
implication: Supports the broader evening short-wavelength light-reduction mechanism, while remaining separate from eyewear claims.
caveat: Small hospital-environment study; not red-light glasses before bed.

headline: Adolescent DSWPD registry shows a clinical circadian-use boundary
implication: Useful for endpoint and pediatric-boundary tracking, not for adult protocol efficacy language.
caveat: The source is registry/protocol context and includes adolescent circadian disorder criteria and co-interventions.

headline: Mania feasibility source is an implementation boundary
implication: Useful for safety and acceptability framing in psychiatric variants, not adult bedtime efficacy.
caveat: Qualitative feasibility study; no source-owned efficacy result.

headline: Pediatric psychiatry review is a boundary source
implication: Supports careful population labeling for youth or psychiatric contexts, not adult protocol efficacy.
caveat: Narrative review with no red-glasses intervention effect estimate.

headline: Pregnancy registry is a special-population boundary source
implication: It supports careful population-boundary language rather than consumer efficacy claims.
caveat: The pregnancy population and registry-only status make it unsuitable as direct adult bedtime protocol evidence.

headline: Elderly mania case is not consumer sleep evidence
implication: Useful to flag psychiatric and age boundaries for blue-blocking glasses.
caveat: Single uncontrolled inpatient case report.

headline: Inpatient mania eyewear registry is supervised psychiatric context
implication: Supports a boundary that bipolar/mania applications are clinical protocols, not casual sleep hacks.
caveat: The source is a registry record and the population, wear schedule, and treatment context are mismatched to the target protocol.

headline: Post-surgical registry context is not bedtime-glasses efficacy evidence
implication: Useful for tracking a supervised hospital variant, but it should not support consumer protocol efficacy claims.
caveat: Registry record only; no source-owned results were extracted and the surgical population is a major mismatch.

headline: Ongoing bipolar eyewear registry is not consumer efficacy evidence
implication: Supports careful clinical-boundary and horizon-scanning language for mood-disorder applications.
caveat: No outcome result is extracted; the population and protocol are clinically supervised and state-adapted.

headline: Digital blue-light safety review is a claim boundary
implication: Useful to avoid overstating eye or visual-performance benefits of glasses.
caveat: No bedtime glasses intervention result.

headline: Multi-component adolescent circadian registry cannot isolate glasses
implication: Use only as context for how evening light reduction may be embedded in broader circadian protocols.
caveat: Bedtime advancement and morning bright light are co-interventions, so eyewear-specific claims would overreach.

headline: Ocular review argues against retinal-protection claims
implication: Use to keep protocol claims focused on sleep/circadian endpoints, not eye-disease prevention.
caveat: Narrative ocular-safety review; no sleep intervention result.

headline: Chromatic filters can alter visual performance
implication: Use as background for safety language around color and contrast changes.
caveat: Older acute visual-performance source with no extracted sleep outcome.

headline: Young-child home-light registry is a pediatric boundary source
implication: Useful for tracking pediatric endpoints and home-light confounders, not for adult claims.
caveat: No results are available from this registry source, and the age group is a major mismatch.

headline: Pediatric psychiatry registry is a supervised-use boundary
implication: Useful for gap tracking and safety language, not for adult self-experiment efficacy claims.
caveat: No registry outcome results are extracted and the intervention includes darkness/dark-mode co-components.

headline: Small screen-time experiment is mixed and age-dependent
implication: Preserve the teenage signal and adult null result separately; use only as low-quality adjacent context.
caveat: Student-led, nonrandomized, six-night pre-post design with small subgroups and nonstandardized sleep tracking.

headline: PROSPERO spectacle-lens review registration is a claim-audit source
implication: Use to avoid overextending eye or retinal-protection claims into the bedtime sleep protocol.
caveat: The registration itself is not a completed review and provides no effect estimate.
